{"lessons": ["

Three verbs of movement

Andare (to go), venire (to come) and uscire (to go out) are irregular, but each one follows a simple logic.

andarevenireuscire
iovadovengoesco
tuvaivieniesci
lui, leivavieneesce
noiandiamoveniamousciamo
voiandateveniteuscite
lorovannovengonoescono

Andare mixes two stems, a bit like English \"go / went\": vado, vai, va, vanno on one side, and andiamo, andate, built on the infinitive, on the other.

Venire changes its stem: vieni, viene, but veniamo, venite. On top of that, a g appears with io and loro: vengo, vengono.

The uscire trap: when the stress falls on the beginning of the word, the u becomes e: esco, esci, esce, escono. Only noi and voi keep the u: usciamo, uscite. \"Uscono\" doesn't exist.

As in English, you use venire (to come) when you're joining the person you're talking to:

Stasera andiamo in pizzeria. Vieni anche tu?Tonight we're going to the pizzeria. Are you coming too?
", "

A, in, da: saying where you're going

With these verbs, three little prepositions are enough. The rule depends on the type of place.

To talk aboutPrepositionExamples
a cityavado a Roma, a Parigi
a country, a regioninvado in Italia, in Sicilia
many everyday placesinin ufficio, in banca, in farmacia, in palestra, in centro, in montagna
a few places to memorizeaa casa, a scuola, a teatro
someone's placedavado da Marco, vengo da Giulia
the city you come fromdavengo da Parigi
means of transportationin / ain macchina, in autobus, a piedi

Two traps for English speakers. English says \"to the bank, to the pharmacy\", with \"the\"; Italian says in banca, in farmacia, with no article. And \"to someone's place\" is always da: vado da Luca (I'm going to Luca's), never \"vado a Luca\".

For origin, you already know Sono di Parigi. With venire, you say da: Vengo da Parigi. And to leave the house: uscire di casa.

Oggi vado in ufficio a piedi, e stasera vado da Paola.Today I'm going to the office on foot, and tonight I'm going to Paola's place.

title: Andare, venire, uscire
topic: present tense of andare, venire, uscire; a, in, da with places
why: First lesson of the irregular-verbs unit: andare, venire and uscire are used every day, and the learner has already written "uscono" for escono and mixed up the prepositions of place. The forms and the simple prepositions (a, in, da) are locked in before the articulated prepositions.
